title: Infinitely Many Primes ≡ 1 (mod 4): Euler's Criterion Proof
description: Answers Open Question 3 from 'Infinitely Many Primes ≡ 3 (mod 4)': proves there are infinitely many primes ≡ 1 (mod 4) using Euler's quadratic residue criterion. The construction N = (2·(n+1)!)² + 1 forces all odd prime factors to satisfy p ≡ 1 (mod 4), since p ∣ k²+1 means -1 is a square mod p, which Euler's criterion equates to p ≡ 1 (mod 4). This is the harder companion to the elementary 3 (mod 4) case: no product-mod-4 argument suffices; quadratic residues are essential. 3 theorems, 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext: This answers the natural companion question to Euclid's argument for primes $\equiv 3 \pmod 4$: can the same elementary approach handle primes $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$? The answer requires a genuinely different ingredient: Euler's criterion (1748) that $-1$ is a quadratic residue modulo an odd prime $p$ if and only if $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. This criterion was proved by Euler using Fermat's little theorem (order of the multiplicative group is $p-1$, and $-1$ has order 2, so it lies in a square iff $2 \mid (p-1)/2$ iff $4 \mid p-1$). The construction $N = (2 \cdot (n+1)!)^2 + 1$ is the key: every prime factor $p$ of $N$ satisfies $p \mid k^2 + 1$ for $k = 2 \cdot (n+1)!$, forcing $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ via Euler's criterion. This argument appears in Hardy & Wright's *An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers* and is the prototypical example of how quadratic residues unlock arithmetic progressions beyond the reach of multiplicative congruence arguments.
overview.problemStatement: Open Question 3 from `infinitude-primes-4k3`: prove there are infinitely many primes $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ using an elementary argument. Formally: $\forall n : \mathbb{N},\ \exists p : \mathbb{N},\ \text{Prime}(p) \wedge p > n \wedge p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$.
overview.text: The key asymmetry between the two cases: for $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, a simple product-mod-4 argument works (the set $\{1, 3\}$ under multiplication mod 4 means any integer $\equiv 3 \pmod 4$ must have an odd number of prime factors $\equiv 3 \pmod 4$). For $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, no such direct argument exists — products of primes $\equiv 3 \pmod 4$ can also be $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$ (e.g., $3 \times 3 = 9 \equiv 1$). The fix: use $N = (2 \cdot (n+1)!)^2 + 1$. Any prime $p \mid N$ satisfies $p \mid k^2 + 1$ where $k = 2(n+1)!$, so $k^2 \equiv -1 \pmod p$, making $-1$ a square mod $p$. Euler's criterion then gives $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. The bound $p > n$ follows from the usual factorial argument: if $p \leq n+1$ then $p \mid (n+1)!$, so $p \mid 2(n+1)!$, so $p \mid N - (2(n+1)!)^2 = 1$, contradicting primality.
overview.proofStrategy: Lean proof: `prime_dvd_sq_add_one_mod_four` constructs `IsSquare (-1 : ZMod p)` using $k$ as witness (from $k^2 + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod p$), then applies Mathlib's `Nat.Prime.mod_four_ne_three_of_dvd_isSquare_neg_one`. Main theorem: `exists_odd_prime_factor` gives an odd prime dividing $N$ (which is odd), then `prime_dvd_sq_add_one_mod_four` gives $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and contradiction for $p \leq n$ via `Nat.dvd_factorial` and `Nat.Prime.not_dvd_one`.
keyInsights: The Euclid-style argument for $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ uses the multiplicative closure $1 \cdot 1 \equiv 1 \pmod 4$; this fails for $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ because $3 \cdot 3 \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, so a product of primes $\equiv 3$ can be $\equiv 1$.

The construction $N = (2k)^2 + 1$ is the key: any prime factor $p$ of $N$ satisfies $p \mid (2k)^2 + 1$, i.e., $(2k)^2 \equiv -1 \pmod p$, making $-1$ a square mod $p$. This is a genuine quadratic constraint, not a multiplicative congruence.

Euler's criterion ($-1$ is a square mod $p$ iff $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$) is the bridge between the divisibility condition and the modular constraint. In Mathlib, this is `Nat.Prime.mod_four_ne_three_of_dvd_isSquare_neg_one` from `Mathlib.NumberTheory.SumTwoSquares`.

The use of $(2 \cdot (n+1)!)^2 + 1$ rather than $(p_1 \cdots p_k)^2 + 1$ avoids the finiteness assumption: we directly construct a number with prime factors $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$ exceeding $n$, without needing to assume finiteness of the set of such primes.

This is a special case of Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions, but requires none of the analytic machinery (L-functions, Dirichlet characters). The same quadratic residue ingredient underlies Fermat's two-square theorem: primes $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$ are exactly those expressible as $a^2 + b^2$.
prerequisites: Euler's criterion: -1 is a QR mod p iff p ≡ 1 (mod 4) for odd primes p

conclusion.summary: Proves infinitely many primes $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$ via $N = (2 \cdot (n+1)!)^2 + 1$ and Euler's quadratic residue criterion. Answers OQ-03 from `infinitude-primes-4k3`. 3 theorems, 0 axioms, fully machine-verified. The proof is the definitive answer to why the elementary $p \equiv 3$ argument does not directly extend: quadratic residues are necessary and sufficient.
conclusion.implications: Together with `infinitude-primes-4k3`, this proof covers all non-trivial residue classes mod 4 by elementary means: $p \equiv 1$ needs Euler's criterion; $p \equiv 3$ needs only product-mod-4 arithmetic. This contrast illustrates the general phenomenon in Dirichlet's theorem: some arithmetic progressions admit purely multiplicative proofs, others require deeper algebraic machinery. The quadratic residue criterion used here is the same ingredient underlying Fermat's two-square theorem and the splitting of primes in the Gaussian integers $\mathbb{Z}[i]$.
openQuestions: Can Fermat's theorem on sums of two squares be formalized using this same Mathlib infrastructure: $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4 \iff p = a^2 + b^2$? Mathlib already has the criterion (`Nat.Prime.mod_four_ne_three_of_dvd_isSquare_neg_one`); the remaining step is constructing the explicit decomposition.

What is the density of primes $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$ among all primes? Dirichlet's theorem guarantees density $1/\phi(4) = 1/2$, but proving this requires analytic tools (L-functions, Prime Number Theorem for arithmetic progressions) far beyond the elementary methods here.

sections.title: Imports and Context

sections.title: Key Lemma: Odd Primes Dividing k² + 1 Are ≡ 1 (mod 4)
sections.summary: prime_dvd_sq_add_one_mod_four: if an odd prime p divides k²+1, then p ≡ 1 (mod 4). Proof: constructs IsSquare(-1 : ZMod p) from the divisibility (k is the witness: k² = -1 in ZMod p), applies Mathlib's Euler criterion to get p ≢ 3 (mod 4), then casework on {1,3} gives p ≡ 1.

sections.title: Helper: Odd Numbers Have Odd Prime Factors
sections.summary: exists_odd_prime_factor: any odd number > 1 has an odd prime factor. Uses Nat.exists_prime_and_dvd for existence, then shows factor cannot be 2 (contradicts oddness).

sections.title: Main Theorem and Infinitude
sections.summary: infinitely_many_primes_1_mod_4: for every n, exists prime p > n with p ≡ 1 (mod 4). Construction N = (2(n+1)!)²+1 (odd, > 1), factor p via exists_odd_prime_factor, apply key lemma for p ≡ 1 mod 4, derive p > n by contradiction via Nat.dvd_factorial + not_dvd_one. primes_1_mod_4_infinite follows via Set.infinite_iff_exists_gt.
